Chapter 7: Navigating School and Work with Dyslexia
As we move through life, the ways we experience dyslexia—and the ways we can thrive with it—begin to shift. Let’s take a look at some practical strategies for doing well in both school and at work, with an emphasis on self-advocacy, planning ahead, and knowing how to ask for the right support.
In school, students with dyslexia have some powerful tools at their disposal, like individualized education plans, or IEPs, and 504 plans. These plans outline the specific supports and modifications that can make learning more accessible. The key is understanding how to work with teachers and school administrators, so those needs don’t get overlooked.
Here are a few strategies that really make a difference:
First, don’t be afraid to request accommodations. That could mean extra time on tests, getting access to audiobooks, or even doing assignments in a way that plays to your strengths. Little changes like these can level the playing field.
Second, find ways to organize information. Maybe you love graphic organizers, mind maps, or color-coded notes. These tools help break down complex material so it’s easier to understand and remember.
And most importantly, communicate your needs. If sitting near the front helps you focus, or if you need instructions repeated, just say so. Speaking up about what works best for you can make all the difference.
Now, let’s talk about the workplace. The challenges change, but so do the opportunities. Many adults with dyslexia discover that their unique skills—like creative problem-solving or thinking outside the box—are actually huge assets, especially in fields that value fresh perspectives.
Of course, there are still tasks that might feel tricky, like reading through dense reports or writing long, detailed emails. But here’s some practical advice:
Lean on assistive technology. Things like speech-to-text software, digital calendars, or project management apps can make everyday tasks smoother and less stressful.
Remember, it’s okay to delegate or collaborate. Focus on the roles that play to your strengths, and don’t hesitate to team up with people whose skills complement your own.
And keep learning. Jump at opportunities for professional development, and if you need extra training or support, ask for it. Continuous learning is key.
There are plenty of inspiring real-world examples out there. Imagine a graphic designer who uses their visual thinking skills to create amazing marketing materials. Or a manager who’s fantastic at motivating teams and seeing the big picture. These are just a couple of ways people have built successful careers by leaning into their dyslexic strengths.
So, here’s the key takeaway: Dyslexia doesn’t have to limit you—whether you’re in school or building your career. With the right strategies and support, it’s absolutely possible to thrive in any environment.
